settings.pmProfile:
Barrister Iftikhar Gillani was sworn in as the 17th Prime Minister of the Azad Government of the State of Jammu & Kashmir and Leader of the House on 28 August 2026, elected by a large majority of the AJK Legislative Assembly.

## Priorities of the government

Since taking office, the Prime Minister has set out the priorities of his government in public meetings and statements:

- Strengthening the rule of law and coordination between the bar and the bench, so that justice is delivered effectively.
- Modern, transparent and accessible digital services, starting with a working official portal of the Government of AJK.
- Recruitment in government institutions strictly on merit, under the Third Party Recruitment Act.
- Better health and education services, infrastructure and employment opportunities in every constituency.
settings.mission: To give effective leadership, in coordination with the departments and subordinate offices of the government, in forming and carrying out a complete strategy for the quick handling and disposal of government business for the convenience of the public.
settings.vision: To create a people-friendly atmosphere, in line with the vision of the Azad Government of the State of Jammu & Kashmir, with better public service delivery and an efficient, sustainable and fair approach to address and resolve the issues of the people of the State and meet their needs through good governance.
settings.causeTitle: The Base Camp of the Freedom Struggle
settings.causeText: Azad Jammu & Kashmir was liberated by its own people in 1947. Ever since, it has stood as the base camp of the struggle of the people of Jammu & Kashmir for their right of self-determination, as promised to them by the resolutions of the United Nations Security Council.
settings.causeQuote: The question of the accession of Jammu and Kashmir to India or Pakistan should be decided through the democratic method of a free and impartial plebiscite.
settings.glanceIntro: The State of Jammu & Kashmir, with an area of 84,471 square miles, lies to the north east of Pakistan and the north west of India, and shares borders with China and Afghanistan to the north. At the time of Partition it was the largest of the 562 princely states of the subcontinent, and it still claims that status. Its area is almost equal to that of Belgium, Denmark, the Netherlands, Austria and Albania put together, and only slightly smaller than Great Britain.

news.title: Prime Minister pledges stronger rule of law at Kotli District Bar oath-taking
news.body:
Prime Minister Azad Jammu & Kashmir Barrister Iftikhar Gillani on Sunday said his government would take steps to strengthen the rule of law in the State and improve coordination between the bar and the bench to ensure the effective delivery of justice.

Addressing the oath-taking ceremony of the newly elected office bearers of the District Bar Association Kotli, he said lawyers had an important role in upholding the Constitution, the rule of law and access to justice.

He said the government was taking steps to address public issues and provide basic amenities, adding that all available resources would be used to resolve the problems facing Kotli. He assured the legal fraternity that its legitimate issues would be taken up at the relevant forums and that the necessary steps would be taken to resolve them.

Later, the Prime Minister administered the oath to the newly elected office bearers and congratulated them. District Bar Association President Khawaja Haq Nawaz Butt apprised the Prime Minister of the problems faced by lawyers and sought government support to resolve them.

The ceremony was attended by the Speaker of the AJK Legislative Assembly, Chaudhry Tariq Farooq, ministers, members of the Assembly and lawyers.

news.title: Prime Minister directs IT department to make the official AJK portal operational
news.body:
Prime Minister Azad Kashmir Barrister Iftikhar Gillani has directed officials of the IT department to redouble their efforts to make the official portal of the Government of AJK operational at the earliest, ensuring access to all services being provided digitally.

He said this while addressing a meeting convened to review matters related to making the official portal operational. The Prime Minister said the government was moving towards modern, transparent and accessible digital services. He emphasised that the experience and expertise of the Punjab IT Board should be used to strengthen digital governance in Azad Kashmir.

During the meeting, officials of the IT department briefed the Prime Minister on the establishment of the portal, the progress made so far and the plans for providing government services online.

The meeting was attended by Principal Secretary Adnan Khurshid, Secretary IT and Information Muhammad Rashid Hanif, Additional Director General Punjab IT Board Muhammad Kashif Farooq, Programme Manager Noreen Anwar and Waqar Ali.

news.title: Government to focus on health, education, infrastructure and jobs in every constituency
news.body:
Prime Minister Azad Kashmir Barrister Iftikhar Gillani has said that the government will focus on improving health and education services, infrastructure and employment opportunities across all constituencies.

He said this during a meeting with a delegation from the Lachhrat constituency, which called on him under the leadership of former minister Chaudhry Shahzad Mahmood. The Prime Minister said that recruitment in government institutions would be made strictly on merit under the Third Party Recruitment Act.

During the meeting, the delegation apprised Prime Minister Iftikhar Gillani of the issues faced by the people of the Lachhrat constituency. The delegation also invited the Prime Minister to visit the constituency, which he accepted.

On the occasion, Chaudhry Shahzad Mahmood thanked the Prime Minister for accepting the invitation.

timeline.title: Treaty of Amritsar
timeline.text: After defeating the Sikhs, the British sold Kashmir to Gulab Singh of Jammu for Rs. 7.5 million, beginning a century of Dogra rule.

timeline.title: 13 July Martyrs
timeline.text: 22 Kashmiris were martyred outside Srinagar Central Jail while calling the azan, marking the start of the organised freedom movement. 13 July is observed as Martyrs' Day.

timeline.title: Muslim Conference founded
timeline.text: The All Jammu & Kashmir Muslim Conference, the first political party of the State, was formed to give the people a political voice.

timeline.title: Resolution of Accession to Pakistan
timeline.text: On 19 July 1947 the Muslim Conference resolved in Srinagar that the State should accede to Pakistan.

timeline.title: Azad Government established
timeline.text: On 24 October 1947 the people liberated this part of the State and formed the Azad Government, with Sardar Muhammad Ibrahim Khan as its first President.

timeline.title: Kashmir at the United Nations
timeline.text: India took the Kashmir question to the UN Security Council on 1 January 1948. Resolution 47 of 21 April 1948 called for a free and impartial plebiscite.

timeline.title: Ceasefire and UNCIP resolutions
timeline.text: The UN brokered a ceasefire on 1 January 1949. The UNCIP resolutions of 13 August 1948 and 5 January 1949 set out the terms of the plebiscite.

timeline.title: Simla Agreement
timeline.text: The ceasefire line became the Line of Control. The agreement kept the final settlement of Jammu & Kashmir as an outstanding question.

timeline.title: Interim Constitution
timeline.text: The AJK Interim Constitution introduced a parliamentary system with an elected Legislative Assembly, President and Prime Minister.

timeline.title: Earthquake and rebuilding
timeline.text: The 8 October 2005 earthquake devastated Muzaffarabad, Bagh and other districts. The people of AJK rebuilt their homes, schools and towns.

timeline.title: 5 August 2019
timeline.text: India revoked Articles 370 and 35A in Indian Illegally Occupied Jammu & Kashmir. AJK observes the day as Youm-e-Istehsal (Day of Exploitation).

pages.title: The Kashmir Cause
pages.subtitle: Kashmir: the oldest dispute on the UN agenda
pages.body:
## Kashmir, the oldest dispute on the UN agenda

The Kashmir dispute is the oldest unresolved international conflict in the world today. Pakistan considers Kashmir its core political dispute with India, and so does the international community, except India.

India's forcible occupation of the State of Jammu and Kashmir in 1947 is the main cause of the dispute. India claims that the Maharaja of Kashmir "signed" a controversial document, the Instrument of Accession, on 26 October 1947, in return for India's military help against a popular uprising. The people of Kashmir and Pakistan do not accept the Indian claim, and there are doubts about the very existence of the Instrument of Accession. The United Nations does not consider the Indian claim legally valid: it recognises Kashmir as a disputed territory. With the exception of India, the entire world community recognises Kashmir as a disputed territory.

All the principles on which the Indian subcontinent was partitioned by the British in 1947 justify Kashmir becoming a part of Pakistan: the State had a Muslim-majority population, it was geographically contiguous with Pakistan, and it had essential economic links with the territories that make up Pakistan.

## History of the dispute

The State of Jammu and Kashmir has historically remained independent, except in the anarchic conditions of the late 18th and first half of the 19th century, or when it was part of the vast empires of the Mauryas (3rd century BC), the Mughals (16th to 18th century) and the British (mid-19th to mid-20th century). All these empires included not only present-day India and Pakistan but other countries of the region as well.

Until 1846, Kashmir was part of the Sikh empire. In that year the British defeated the Sikhs and sold Kashmir to Gulab Singh of Jammu for Rs. 7.5 million under the Treaty of Amritsar. Gulab Singh, the Maharaja, signed a separate treaty with the British which gave him the status of an independent princely ruler of Kashmir. Gulab Singh died in 1857 and was succeeded by Ranbir Singh (1857-1885). Two other Maharajas, Partab Singh (1885-1925) and Hari Singh (1925-1949), ruled in succession.

Gulab Singh and his successors ruled Kashmir in a tyrannical and repressive way. The people of Kashmir, nearly 80 per cent of whom were Muslims, rose against Maharaja Hari Singh's rule. He ruthlessly crushed a mass uprising in 1931. In 1932, Sheikh Abdullah and Chaudhry Ghulam Abbas formed Kashmir's first political party, the All Jammu & Kashmir Muslim Conference (a faction of which was renamed the National Conference in 1939). In 1934 the Maharaja gave way and allowed limited democracy in the form of a Legislative Assembly. However, unease with the Maharaja's rule continued.

Under the plan for the partition of India, the rulers of princely states were given the choice to accede to either India or Pakistan, or to remain independent. They were, however, advised to accede to the contiguous dominion, taking geographical and ethnic factors into account.

In Kashmir, however, the Maharaja hesitated. The mainly Muslim population, having seen the early and covert arrival of Indian troops, rebelled, and events slipped out of the Maharaja's hands. The people of Kashmir were demanding to join Pakistan. The Maharaja eventually gave way to Indian pressure and agreed to join India by, as India claims, "signing" the controversial Instrument of Accession on 26 October 1947. Kashmir was provisionally accepted into the Indian Union pending a free and impartial plebiscite. This was spelled out in a letter from the Governor General of India, Lord Mountbatten, to the Maharaja on 27 October 1947. In that letter, accepting the accession, Mountbatten made it clear that the State would only be incorporated into the Indian Union after a reference had been made to the people of Kashmir. Having accepted the principle of a plebiscite, India has since obstructed every attempt to hold one.

In 1947 India and Pakistan went to war over Kashmir. During the war it was India which first took the Kashmir dispute to the United Nations, on 1 January 1948. A year later, on 1 January 1949, the UN helped bring about a ceasefire between the two countries. The ceasefire line was renamed the Line of Control under the Simla Agreement of 1972.

With the mutual consent of India and Pakistan, the UN Security Council (UNSC) and the UN Commission for India and Pakistan (UNCIP) passed several resolutions in the years following the 1947-48 war. The UNSC Resolution of 21 April 1948, one of the principal UN resolutions on Kashmir, stated that "both India and Pakistan desire that the question of the accession of Jammu and Kashmir to India or Pakistan should be decided through the democratic method of a free and impartial plebiscite". Later UNSC resolutions reiterated the same position. The UNCIP resolutions of 13 August 1948 and 5 January 1949 reinforced the UNSC resolutions.

## The Kashmir issue in a nutshell

The current struggle in Indian Illegally Occupied Jammu & Kashmir (IIOJK) is rooted in the struggle of the people for the exercise of their right of self-determination. Peaceful processions demanding freedom have been fired upon by the Indian Army and police. Thousands of men, women and children have been killed or wounded.

New Delhi's allegation of assistance to the Kashmiri people from the Pakistan side is unfounded. Objective reports in the foreign media testify that the Kashmiri movement is indigenous.

Pakistan upholds the right of the people of Jammu and Kashmir to self-determination in accordance with the resolutions of the UN Security Council. These resolutions of 1948 and 1949 provide for a free and impartial plebiscite to determine the future of the State by the people of Jammu and Kashmir.

The basic points about the UN resolutions are:

- The complaint relating to Kashmir was initiated by India in the Security Council.
- The Council, explicitly and by implication, rejected India's claim that Kashmir is legally Indian territory.
- The resolutions established self-determination as the governing principle for the settlement of the Kashmir dispute. This is the world body's commitment to the people of Kashmir.
- The resolutions endorsed a binding agreement between India and Pakistan, reached through the mediation of UNCIP, that a plebiscite would be held under agreed and specified conditions.
- The Security Council has rejected the Indian contention that the people of Kashmir have exercised their right of self-determination by taking part in the "elections" which India has organised from time to time in the occupied territory. The very low turnout in the 1989 "elections" was a clear repudiation of the Indian claim.
- Pakistan continues to adhere to the UN resolutions. They are binding on India as well.

## The Simla Agreement

The Simla Agreement of 2 July 1972, to which Pakistan also continues to adhere, did not alter the status of Jammu and Kashmir as a disputed territory:

- Para 6 of the Agreement lists "a final settlement of Jammu and Kashmir" as one of the outstanding questions awaiting settlement.
- Para 4 (ii) speaks of a "Line of Control" as distinguished from an international border. It also explicitly protects "the recognized position of either side". The recognised position of Pakistan is the one recognised by the United Nations and the world community in general.
- Article 1 (iv) clearly refers to the Kashmir issue when it speaks of "the basic issues and causes of conflict which have bedevilled the relations between the two countries for the last 25 years".

pages.title: AJK at a Glance
pages.subtitle: The land, the people and the story of the Azad State
pages.body:
## The State of Jammu & Kashmir

The Muslims of Jammu & Kashmir began a war of liberation in 1947. As a result, the Azad Government of the State of Jammu & Kashmir was established on 24 October 1947 in the liberated area, about 5,000 square miles of the State's total area of 84,471 square miles. An area of about 28,000 square miles was also liberated by the Gilgit Scouts; it now forms Gilgit-Baltistan, administered by the Federal Government of Pakistan.

## How the government developed

The government established on 24 October 1947 worked like a war council. Rules of Business were framed to run the administration, under which both executive and legislative authority was vested in the President. The Courts and Laws Code was enacted in 1948 to run the judicial administration, and some laws of the former State of Jammu & Kashmir were allowed to continue. The Rules of Business were revised in 1952, setting out the system of administration and legislation, and revised again in 1957.

From 1947 to 1960, the person who held the confidence of the Working Committee of the Muslim Conference was nominated as President of Azad Jammu & Kashmir. In the early years there was also the office of Supreme Head, who approved legislation, but it was abolished in 1952. After that the President alone was the Executive Head, assisted by ministers.

In 1960 a presidential election system through the votes of Basic Democrats was introduced, with a body known as the Azad Jammu & Kashmir State Council, also elected by the Basic Democrats. The Council had 12 members elected by the people of Azad Jammu & Kashmir and 12 elected by the refugees of the State settled in Pakistan. In 1964 this system was replaced by the Azad Jammu & Kashmir Government Act, 1964, under which 8 State Councillors were elected by the Basic Democrats of Azad Jammu & Kashmir. In 1965 provision was made for two members to be nominated by the President from among the refugees settled in Pakistan.

## The parliamentary system

The Azad Jammu & Kashmir Interim Constitution of 1974 introduced the parliamentary system that continues today: an elected Legislative Assembly, a President as Head of State, and a Prime Minister as the chief executive, chosen by the Assembly as Leader of the House. Abdul Hamid Khan became the first Prime Minister in 1975.
